Enquiry 1: Young Queen Victoria, Steam Railways and Shrinking Britain (1837–1860)

Big Question: How did steam railways and penny post shrink Queen Victoria’s Britain?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Locomotive (Lo-co-mo-tive) Railway Mania (Rail-way Ma-ni-a) Railway Time (Rail-way Time) Penny Black (Pen-ny Black) Constitutional Monarch (Con-sti-tu-tion-al Mon-arch)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: George and Robert Stephenson’s Steam Locomotive Rocket (Science Museum, London)
Steam & Time Clue: Fast inter-city locomotives forced Britain to adopt shared Greenwich Railway Time and carried 1840 Penny Black mail overnight!

1a. Look closely at Source B. How did Rowland Hill’s 1840 Penny Black make posting letters fairer for poor families?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source B, Rowland Hill’s 1840 Penny Black stamp transformed letter-writing for poor families because..."
Word Bank: May 1840 • Penny Black • one penny • V.R. pillar boxes
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Queen Victoria becomes the first British monarch to ride a steam train from Slough to Paddington (June 1842)
Eighteen-year-old Princess Victoria inherits the British throne upon the death of King William IV (June 1837)
Great Western Railway and major lines adopt standard Greenwich 'Railway Time' across stations (1840–1847)
Rowland Hill launches the world’s first sticky stamp, the one-penny Penny Black (May 1840)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?

Enquiry 2: Chimneys, Cotton Mills and Children Underground (1837–1850)

Big Question: Why was factory and coal-mine work so dangerous for Victorian children?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Cottonopolis (Cot-ton-op-o-lis) Piecer (Piec-er) Scavenger (Scav-en-ger) Trapper (Trap-per) Hurrier (Hur-ri-er)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Thomas Allom’s Engraving of a Lancashire Power-Loom Weaving Shed (1835)
1842 Mines Clue: Printed woodcuts of chained child hurriers and eight-year-old trappers persuaded MPs to ban all females and boys under ten underground!

1a. Study Source B. What does this 1842 woodcut reveal about the work of child "hurriers" underground?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source B, the 1842 Royal Commission woodcut reveals that child hurriers underground..."
Word Bank: hurriers • corves • leather belt and chain • low coal seam
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Victorian Census reveals more Britons live in towns and cities than in the countryside for the first time (1851)
Humphry Davy invents the wire-gauze miner’s safety lamp to reduce underground firedamp blasts (1815)
Royal Commission inspectors interview eight-year-old trapper Sarah Gooder in a Yorkshire coal pit (1841–1842)
Steam-powered Lancashire cotton mills expand rapidly across booming 'Cottonopolis' Manchester (1830s)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?

Enquiry 3: Workhouses, Ragged Schools and Champions of Reform (1834–1880)

Big Question: How did Victorian reformers rescue children from workhouses, pits, and streets?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Workhouse (Work-house) Gruel (Gru-el) Oakum (Oak-um) Factory Inspector (Fac-to-ry In-spec-tor) Ragged School (Rag-ged School)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: George Cruikshank’s Etching "Oliver Asking for More" in Oliver Twist (1838)
Workhouse Clue: Splitting husbands, wives, and children onto watery gruel and tarred oakum-picking made the 1834 workhouse deeply feared!

1a. Inspect Source A. How did Cruikshank and Dickens make readers feel sympathy for workhouse children?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, George Cruikshank and Charles Dickens stirred sympathy for workhouse children by..."
Word Bank: 1834 Poor Law • Oliver Twist • gruel • separate wards
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Ten-year-old orphan Jim Jarvis leads Thomas Barnardo across freezing East London rooftops, inspiring Barnardo’s Homes (1870)
Poor Law Amendment Act groups parishes to build strict, family-splitting Union Workhouses (1834)
Parliament passes the Ten Hours Act limiting women and teenagers in textile mills to ten hours a day (1847)
Lord Shaftesbury’s Mines and Collieries Act bans all females and boys under ten from working underground (1842)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?

Enquiry 4: Inside a Victorian Classroom — Slates, Drill and the 1870 School Act (1870–1901)

Big Question: What was daily life really like inside a strict Victorian classroom?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Board School (Board School) Three Rs (Three Rs) Copperplate (Cop-per-plate) Dunce’s Cap (Dun-ce’s Cap) Drill (Drill)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Wooden-Framed Victorian Classroom Writing Slate (c. 1890–1900)
Classroom Clue: Reusable Welsh slates saved costly paper and ink until older pupils mastered neat right-handed copperplate handwriting!

1a. Inspect Source A. Why did Victorian schools give younger children framed slates instead of paper books?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, Victorian teachers gave younger pupils wooden-framed Welsh slates because..."
Word Bank: Welsh slates • paper • inkwells • copperplate
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Parliament abolishes weekly 'school pence' fees so elementary Board Schools become free (1891)
William Forster’s Elementary Education Act sets up local School Boards to build missing schools (1870)
School leaving age rises to twelve as Victorian literacy climbs above ninety-five per cent (1899)
Mundella’s Education Act makes school attendance compulsory for children aged five to ten (1880)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?

Enquiry 5: Workshop of the World — The 1851 Crystal Palace and Dazzling Inventions (1851–1901)

Big Question: Why did the 1851 Crystal Palace and new inventions amaze the world?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Crystal Palace (Crys-tal Pal-ace) Workshop of the World (Work-shop of the World) Electric Telegraph (E-lec-tric Tel-e-graph) Incandescent Bulb (In-can-des-cent Bulb) Algorithm (Al-go-rith-m)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Colour Lithograph of the Great Exhibition Transept Inside the Crystal Palace (1851)
1851 Clue: Cheap shilling excursion trains let working families see 100,000 inventions—and profits funded South Kensington’s great museums!

1a. Inspect Source A. What made Joseph Paxton’s 1851 Crystal Palace building seem almost magical to visitors?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, Joseph Paxton’s 1851 Crystal Palace in Hyde Park amazed six million visitors because..."
Word Bank: Joseph Paxton • 300,000 glass panes • 100,000 • Science Museum
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Sir Joseph Swan demonstrates his glowing incandescent carbon-filament electric lightbulb in Newcastle (1878–1879)
Ada Lovelace publishes the world’s first computer algorithm for Charles Babbage’s Analytical Engine (1843)
Alexander Graham Bell patents the electric telephone transmitting human speech along wires (1876)
Queen Victoria and Prince Albert open the Great Exhibition inside Hyde Park’s Crystal Palace (1 May 1851)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?

Enquiry 6: Rich and Poor Homes, Seaside Holidays and Victoria’s 63-Year Legacy (1850–1901)

Big Question: How much had daily life changed across Britain by January 1901?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Back-to-Back Houses (Back-to-Back Hous-es) Bank Holidays (Bank Hol-i-days) Bathing Machine (Bath-ing Ma-chine) Penny-Farthing (Pen-ny-Far-thing) Diamond Jubilee (Dia-mond Ju-bi-lee)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: High-Wheeled Victorian "Penny-Farthing" Bicycle (Coventry Transport Museum)
Leisure Clue: Equal-wheeled chain-driven safety bicycles, 1871 Bank Holidays, and Saturday FA Cup football opened outdoor leisure to millions!

1a. Inspect Source A. Why did 1885 chain-driven "safety bicycles" quickly replace this tall penny-farthing?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, the high-wheeled penny-farthing was soon replaced by the 1885 safety bicycle because..."
Word Bank: penny-farthing • five feet high • safety bicycle • 1885
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Queen Victoria dies at Osborne House aged 81 after a 63-year reign over a transformed Britain (22 Jan 1901)
Parliament passes the Bank Holidays Act giving workers four guaranteed paid public holidays (1871)
Huge crowds outside St Paul’s Cathedral celebrate Queen Victoria’s sixty-year Diamond Jubilee (June 1897)
John Kemp Starley’s chain-driven Rover 'safety bicycle' replaces tall, wobbly penny-farthings (1885)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?
